case.narrative: 14-year-8-month-old male with dysmorphic features and history of developmental delay, learning difficulties, disruptive behaviors, and reported regression of learning. Born at 35 weeks gestation to a 21-year-old G1P0 mother; prenatal ultrasounds normal; no maternal medication use reported. Birth weight 2637 g; mild neonatal jaundice; 5-day hospitalization for breathing difficulties. Motor/language milestones delayed (sat at 1 year, walked at 13–14 months, first words at 3.5 years). Diagnosed with ADHD at age 8. At genetic evaluation: weight 47.2 kg (20th %ile), height 162 cm (22nd %ile), head circumference 53.2 cm (30th %ile). Craniofacial findings: dolichocephaly with prominent occiput; long narrow face; heavy eyebrows with medial flare; sparse fine scalp hair; telecanthus (ICD 3.9 cm); very soft ear cartilage with Darwinian tubercle bilaterally; esotropia; narrow/short philtrum; bifid uvula; high palate; broad nose (mid and tip); receding anterior hairline with widow’s peak. Pubertal development barely beginning Tanner II. Other findings: hyperconvexed nails; collapsed foot arches; slight scoliosis; large-appearing elbows with prominent carrying angles; dry skin with eczema on dorsum; numerous moles (notably under left eye). Educational history: in 8th grade in special education, functioning around a 2nd grade level.

case.narrative: A 6-year-old girl fell at school onto an outstretched hand. She previously sustained a mid-shaft both-bone forearm fracture treated with flexible intramedullary titanium elastic nails 5 months earlier. On presentation to the emergency department she had an obvious right upper limb deformity but denied pain; this was an isolated injury, she was clinically stable, and distal neurovascular status was intact. X-rays showed a new fracture through the prior fracture site with intramedullary nails in place. She underwent closed reduction under general anesthesia with correction of nail angulation to achieve acceptable alignment, was discharged the next day, and follow-up confirmed radiographic and clinical union. Intramedullary nails were removed 6 months after the new injury.
